name: US-typical
jurisdiction: United States, general patterns (state and local law varies)
summary: Common US residential lease patterns. State and city rules differ a lot; treat every flag as a prompt to check your local law or a tenant union.

rules.title: Late fee size
rules.note: Many US states cap or regulate residential late fees, often as a percentage of monthly rent. Fees well above about 5% of rent are frequently treated as unreasonable penalties.
rules.ask: Can the late fee be reduced to a fixed percentage of rent that matches our state's rules?
rules.source: General US pattern; check your state landlord-tenant statute.
rules.green: The late fee is a modest share of rent.

rules.title: Grace period before late fees
rules.note: Several states require a grace period (commonly around 5 days) before a late fee can be charged. A fee on day one is a common source of disputes.
rules.ask: Can we add a grace period of at least 5 days before any late fee applies?
rules.source: General US pattern; check your state landlord-tenant statute.
rules.green: There is a grace period before late fees apply.

rules.title: Security deposit size
rules.note: Many states cap security deposits, often at one or two months' rent. Larger deposits are worth questioning.
rules.ask: What is the legal maximum deposit here, and can the deposit be reduced to one month's rent?
rules.source: General US pattern; check your state deposit statute.
rules.green: The deposit is within a common range.

rules.title: Mandatory fees on top of rent
rules.note: Required monthly fees raise your true cost above the advertised rent. The FTC has taken action against large landlords over rental fees that were not disclosed in advertised prices.
rules.ask: Which of these fees are optional, and what is the full monthly amount I must pay including every required fee?
rules.source: FTC: Invitation Homes, $48M settlement over hidden rental fees (2024); Progress Residential / Pretium, $49.75M (November 2026).

rules.title: Automatic renewal
rules.note: Auto-renewal clauses can lock you into another full term if you miss a notice deadline. Some states require landlords to remind tenants about them.
rules.ask: Can the lease convert to month-to-month at the end of the term instead of renewing for a full term?
rules.source: General US pattern; some states regulate automatic renewal clauses.
rules.green: The lease does not renew automatically.

rules.title: Notice to leave
rules.note: 30 to 60 days is common. Longer notice periods, combined with auto-renewal, make it easy to miss the window.
rules.ask: Can the notice period be shortened to 30 days?
rules.green: The notice period is within a common range.

rules.title: Repairs pushed onto the tenant
rules.note: In most states landlords must keep a rental habitable, and that duty generally cannot be waived by lease wording. A 1970s line of cases (for example Javins v. First National Realty, D.C. Cir. 1970) established this implied warranty of habitability.
rules.ask: Which repairs am I responsible for, and will you confirm in writing that you handle structural, plumbing, heating and appliance repairs?
rules.source: Implied warranty of habitability; Javins v. First National Realty Corp., 428 F.2d 1071 (D.C. Cir. 1970).

rules.title: Early termination penalty
rules.note: Penalties of several months' rent are common but negotiable. Many states expect landlords to try to re-rent the unit rather than charge the full remaining rent.
rules.ask: If I need to leave early, will you cap the fee and credit me once the unit is re-rented?
rules.source: General US pattern (duty to mitigate damages varies by state).

rules.title: Possibly unenforceable clause
rules.note: A study of 70 Greater Boston leases found that 51 (73%) contained at least one clause that was unenforceable under state law. Waivers of landlord liability or tenant rights are common examples.
rules.ask: Can we remove the waiver language, since it may not be enforceable here?
